fr.title: Temps des verbes et marqueurs
fr.summary: Au TOEIC, le temps du verbe se devine presque toujours grâce à un marqueur de temps dans la phrase : « ago », « since », « by the time », « currently », « next ». Repère-le d'abord, puis choisis la forme.
keyPoints: **yesterday / last / ago** = prétérit ; **since / for / so far / over the past** = present perfect.
**by the time** + passé = past perfect ; **by next …** = future perfect.
Après **when, if, as soon as, before, until**, on met le **présent** pour parler du futur, jamais « will ».

rules.title: Prétérit ou present perfect
rules.text: Un moment du passé fini (**yesterday, last week, in 2023, two days ago**) demande le prétérit. Une période qui continue jusqu'à maintenant (**since** + point de départ, **for** + durée, **so far, over the past three years, recently, already, yet**) demande le present perfect.

examples.en: We **signed** the contract two weeks ago.
examples.note: « ago » : le moment est fini, donc prétérit.

examples.en: The company **has hired** twelve engineers since January.
examples.note: « since January » : la période court jusqu'à maintenant.

examples.en: Sales **have risen** steadily over the past three years.
examples.note: « over the past three years » : present perfect.

rules.title: Past perfect et future perfect
rules.text: **By the time** + prétérit introduit une action déjà terminée avant : on met le past perfect dans l'autre proposition (« had started »). Pour un futur, **by next June / by the end of the year** appellent le future perfect (« will have + participe »).

examples.en: By the time the manager arrived, the meeting **had** already **started**.
examples.note: Le début de la réunion précède l'arrivée : past perfect.

examples.en: By next June, we **will have opened** five new branches.
examples.note: « by next June » : future perfect.

rules.title: Présent simple, présent continu, futur
rules.text: **usually, every day, always, each month** : présent simple, pour une habitude. **currently, now, at the moment, this week** : présent continu, pour une action en cours. **next, soon, tomorrow, in two weeks** : futur avec « will » ou « be going to ».

examples.en: The warehouse **ships** orders every weekday.
examples.note: « every weekday » : habitude, présent simple.

examples.en: Our team is currently **updating** the customer database.
examples.note: « currently » : action en cours, présent continu.

examples.en: The new manager **will join** us next Monday.
examples.note: « next Monday » : futur avec « will ».

rules.title: Le présent après when, if, as soon as
rules.text: Dans une proposition de temps (**when, as soon as, before, after, until**) ou de condition (**if, unless**), on utilise le présent pour un événement futur. Le verbe de l'autre proposition, lui, est au futur ou à l'impératif.

examples.en: I will call you as soon as the shipment **arrives**.
examples.note: Après « as soon as » : présent, pas « will arrive ».

examples.en: If the flight **is** delayed, we will rebook the hotel.
examples.note: Condition : présent dans la proposition en « if ».

traps.title: Le mauvais temps avec since, for, ago
traps.text: Les options contiennent souvent prétérit et present perfect. « since 2019 », « for ten years » ou « so far » excluent le prétérit simple seul, et « ago » exclut le present perfect (« has left two hours ago » est faux).

traps.title: « will » dans la subordonnée
traps.text: « when she will arrive » et « if the supplier will deliver » sont faux. Exception : « if » au sens de « whether » après « know », « ask » ou « wonder » accepte « will » (« I don't know if she will come »).

traps.title: Un marqueur loin du trou
traps.text: Le marqueur de temps est parfois en début de phrase (« Last year, … ») ou dans la phrase d'à côté. Lis toute la phrase, voire la précédente, avant de choisir parmi les formes conjuguées.

en.title: Verb tenses and time markers
en.summary: On the TOEIC, the verb tense can almost always be guessed from a time marker in the sentence: "ago", "since", "by the time", "currently", "next". Spot it first, then choose the form.
keyPoints: **yesterday / last / ago** = simple past; **since / for / so far / over the past** = present perfect.
**by the time** + past = past perfect; **by next …** = future perfect.
After **when, if, as soon as, before, until**, use the **present** to talk about the future, never "will".

rules.title: Simple past or present perfect
rules.text: A finished moment in the past (**yesterday, last week, in 2023, two days ago**) calls for the simple past. A period that continues up to now (**since** + starting point, **for** + duration, **so far, over the past three years, recently, already, yet**) calls for the present perfect.

examples.en: We **signed** the contract two weeks ago.
examples.note: "ago": the moment is finished, so simple past.

examples.en: The company **has hired** twelve engineers since January.
examples.note: "since January": the period runs up to now.

examples.en: Sales **have risen** steadily over the past three years.
examples.note: "over the past three years": present perfect.

rules.title: Past perfect and future perfect
rules.text: **By the time** + simple past introduces an action already finished before: put the past perfect in the other clause ("had started"). For the future, **by next June / by the end of the year** call for the future perfect ("will have + participle").

examples.en: By the time the manager arrived, the meeting **had** already **started**.
examples.note: The meeting started before the arrival: past perfect.

examples.en: By next June, we **will have opened** five new branches.
examples.note: "by next June": future perfect.

rules.title: Present simple, present continuous, future
rules.text: **usually, every day, always, each month**: present simple, for a habit. **currently, now, at the moment, this week**: present continuous, for an action in progress. **next, soon, tomorrow, in two weeks**: future with "will" or "be going to".

examples.en: The warehouse **ships** orders every weekday.
examples.note: "every weekday": a habit, present simple.

examples.en: Our team is currently **updating** the customer database.
examples.note: "currently": an action in progress, present continuous.

examples.en: The new manager **will join** us next Monday.
examples.note: "next Monday": future with "will".

rules.title: The present after when, if, as soon as
rules.text: In a time clause (**when, as soon as, before, after, until**) or a condition clause (**if, unless**), use the present for a future event. The verb in the other clause is in the future or the imperative.

examples.en: I will call you as soon as the shipment **arrives**.
examples.note: After "as soon as": present, not "will arrive".

examples.en: If the flight **is** delayed, we will rebook the hotel.
examples.note: Condition: present in the "if" clause.

traps.title: The wrong tense with since, for, ago
traps.text: The options often contain the simple past and the present perfect. "since 2019", "for ten years" or "so far" rule out a lone simple past, and "ago" rules out the present perfect ("has left two hours ago" is wrong).

traps.title: "will" in the subordinate clause
traps.text: "when she will arrive" and "if the supplier will deliver" are wrong. Exception: "if" meaning "whether" after "know", "ask" or "wonder" accepts "will" ("I don't know if she will come").

traps.title: A marker far from the blank
traps.text: The time marker is sometimes at the start of the sentence ("Last year, …") or in a neighboring sentence. Read the whole sentence, even the previous one, before choosing among the conjugated forms.
